chapter_name: The Bengal School and Cultural Nationalism
learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how Indian artists rejected Western art during the freedom struggle, using paintbrushes to fight for 'Swadeshi' and national pride!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: During British rule, art schools only taught Western oil painting, treating Indian art as 'inferior'. Abanindranath Tagore rebelled. He created the 'Bengal School' to revive India's glorious artistic past as a form of cultural nationalism.
Instead of copying Europe, Bengal School artists found inspiration in their own heritage: the murals of Ajanta caves, Mughal/Rajput miniatures, and Indian mythology.

Abanindranath invented the 'Wash Technique' (inspired by Japanese artists). After painting with watercolors, the paper was washed in water, softening the lines and creating a hazy, mystical, and poetic atmosphere.

Nandalal Bose, a student of Abanindranath, took art to the masses. He created the famous 'Haripura Posters' for Gandhi's Congress sessions and was chosen to illustrate the original manuscript of the Indian Constitution.

fun_activity.title: 💧 The Wash Experiment
fun_activity.instructions: Paint a simple landscape using watercolors on thick paper. Let it dry completely. Then, take a clean, wet brush and gently brush pure water over the entire painting. Watch how the colors bleed and soften into a hazy 'Bengal School' look!

exam_tips: 📌 'Journey's End' (showing a collapsed camel) was painted by Abanindranath Tagore using the wash technique. It symbolizes the pain and exploitation of India under British rule.
📌 E.B. Havell (a British principal) actually supported Abanindranath in rejecting Western art and reviving Indian traditions.
📌 Always connect the Bengal School with the Swadeshi movement and Cultural Nationalism.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Bengal School was an artistic revolt against Western academic art.
⭐ It pioneered the 'Wash Technique', creating soft, mystical paintings.
⭐ Key figures: Abanindranath Tagore (Founder) and Nandalal Bose (Popularizer).
